---
title: "Custom model design"
---

Suppose several annotators judge whether an event happened, how confident they are, and which event properties apply. The recorded table contains numbers and categories, but the linguistic target is not any one cell. It may be an item level property that the responses measure only indirectly.

The models introduced earlier begin with a response distribution and ask how its parameters vary. A custom model begins one step earlier. It asks which sequence of linguistic states, annotator decisions, and instrument rules could have produced the recorded responses. Familiar probability distributions still supply the pieces. The custom part is their organization through the [joint distributions](../random-variables-and-distributions/joint-probability.qmd) and [conditional independence assumptions](../random-variables-and-distributions/conditional-independence.qmd) introduced earlier.

The recorded annotation and the intended linguistic quantity are different objects. A model connects them only if every probability term corresponds to a defensible part of the annotation process. Additional latent variables do not help merely because they make the model flexible.

## A custom model starts from the instrument

Before writing a likelihood, describe the response protocol.

1. State which question the annotator sees.
2. State which responses are possible.
3. State whether a response controls which question appears next.
4. State which items and annotators contribute repeated responses.
5. State which linguistic quantity the response is intended to measure.

These statements constrain the model. If a follow up appears only after an affirmative gate, its blank cells are generated by the protocol. If annotators use an ordered scale differently, a single item mean may combine item structure with response behavior. The model should represent these facts rather than treating them as details of data cleaning.

## How the module proceeds

We begin with [annotations as measurements](annotations-as-measurements.qmd), which separates a recorded response from the item quantity it is intended to measure. [Data-generating processes](generative-stories.qmd) then order the random steps that connect the two. [Writing a joint model](writing-a-joint-model.qmd) translates those steps into one probability term per choice.

Next, [annotator effects](annotator-effects.qmd) add a stable response tendency only after the item response model is explicit. [Gated annotations](gated-annotations.qmd) represent a protocol in which the availability of a follow up response depends on an earlier answer. [Parameter recovery](parameter-recovery.qmd) tests whether the complete fitting procedure can recover known generating quantities.

The final page combines these pieces in [a UDS measurement model](uds-measurement-model.qmd). Universal Decompositional Semantics is reserved for this application. Earlier pages use schematic annotation tables so that the dataset is not fitted repeatedly while each component is introduced.

## What this module does not reteach

The joint models use [response distributions](../regression-models/generalized-linear-models.qmd), [grouped variation](../regression-models/random-effects.qmd), [posterior computation](../statistical-inference/markov-chain-monte-carlo.qmd), and [posterior predictive checks](../statistical-inference/posterior-predictive-checks.qmd) introduced earlier in the course. Those methods are prerequisites rather than new topics here. We focus instead on which pieces belong together and what each latent quantity means for the annotation process.

This scope keeps the model subordinate to the measurement argument. The goal is not to create the most elaborate probability program. It is to write the smallest generative account that represents the recorded instrument and the linguistic target.

## What this module adds

By the end of the module, we should be able to distinguish an annotation from a construct, turn an instrument description into a joint distribution, represent stable annotator tendencies and gated questions, and block an interpretation when parameters cannot be recovered. We begin with the measurement distinction on which every later step depends.
